section.title: One-sided limits and infinite behavior
section.p: Section gave us tools for limits that settle down to a finite number. But limits can fail, or change character, in several different ways.

A graph can approach one value from the left and another from the right. A function can grow without bound near a point. Or the input itself can move farther and farther away, so that we ask what happens at the far ends of the graph.
These are not rare exceptions. They are some of the most important behaviors calculus has to name.

subsection.title: Infinite limits and vertical asymptotes
subsection.p: A limit can fail in a different way. The left and right sides might agree in direction, but the values might not settle near any finite number.

As x gets close to 2, the denominator
gets close to 0, but it remains positive. Dividing 1 by a very small positive number gives a very large positive number.
The values do not approach a finite number. They grow beyond any fixed bound.

This notation needs careful reading. The symbol \infty is not a real number. So this is not a finite limit. It is a way of saying that the function grows without bound.

exercise.title: What does an infinite limit claim, and what does it refuse to claim?

statement.p: The notation \lim_{x\to a}f(x)=\infty says that f(x) can be made larger than any chosen positive number by taking x sufficiently close to a. In your own words, why is this not a finite limit, and why does the sign of a one-sided infinite limit still matter?

hint.p: Infinity is a direction of unbounded growth, not a real-number target. From one side the values may shoot up; from the other they may shoot down. Those are different stories.

exercise.title: What does x\to\infty mean if infinity is not a number?

statement.p: In the coffee model T(t)=70+\frac{90}{t+1}, the temperature approaches room temperature as time grows. In your own words, what does t\to\infty mean, and why is a horizontal asymptote a statement about the far end of a graph rather than a value the function must reach?

hint.p: The input grows without bound; it does not approach a point called infinity. An asymptote is a line the graph approaches. The function may never equal that height at any finite input.

subsection.title: A map of the new behaviors
subsection.p: The word “limit” now covers several related ideas.

md.mrow: \hline \displaystyle \lim_{x\to a}f(x)=L \amp x\text{ approaches }a\text{ from both sides} \amp f(x)\text{ approaches finite }L
\displaystyle \lim_{x\to a^-}f(x)=L \amp x\text{ approaches }a\text{ from the left} \amp f(x)\text{ approaches finite }L
\displaystyle \lim_{x\to a^+}f(x)=L \amp x\text{ approaches }a\text{ from the right} \amp f(x)\text{ approaches finite }L
\displaystyle \lim_{x\to a}f(x)=\infty \amp x\text{ approaches }a \amp f(x)\text{ grows without bound}

subsection.p: These ideas help us describe graphs accurately. But the word “approaches” is still informal. The next section turns it into a test that does not depend on the drawing or the table.
The test is based on a challenge: make the output error smaller than any tolerance I name.

exercise.title: How do you tell a hole from a vertical asymptote?

statement.p: Cancellation can turn a forbidden input into a hole, while a denominator approaching zero without cancellation can produce a vertical asymptote. In your own words, what nearby output behavior distinguishes those two pictures?

hint.p: Near a hole, the values settle toward a finite height with one point missing. Near a vertical asymptote, the values refuse to settle and instead grow without bound.
